goals.label: I think someone may be autistic
acts: Write down what you have noticed: examples, when it happens and what helps.
Tell a doctor or health professional you trust and ask about screening or an evaluation.
Read about the signs and how diagnosis works, then pick one question to bring with you.

goals.label: We just had a diagnosis
acts: Ask the clinician for a written report and their recommendations.
Ask what early intervention, school or other support services exist in your area and how to apply.
Find one person or group who understands, such as a parent group or an autistic-led organization.

goals.label: I am an autistic adult looking for support
acts: Read what autistic-led organizations say about rights, work and everyday life.
Notice what helps you, such as quiet, routine or clear instructions, and write it down so you can ask for it.
If anxiety, sleep or stomach problems get in the way, tell a doctor. These often occur alongside autism.

goals.label: I am worn out as a caregiver
acts: Pick one small thing to drop or share this week, and ask one trusted person for help.
Look for caregiver support or short-term respite care in your area.
If stress, sleep or your mood are suffering, tell your own doctor. You matter too.

goals.label: Sleep, anxiety or mood is hard
acts: For a week, note when it is worst and what seems to help.
Share your notes with a doctor and ask about support for anxiety, depression, sleep or stomach problems.
Look at the resources below for ideas to talk through.

goals.label: I need help with school or work
acts: Write down which supports would help, such as a quiet space, written instructions or extra time.
Ask the school or workplace what support plans or adjustments they offer and how to request them.
Keep a copy of what you ask for and what is agreed.

glossary: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)
A neurodevelopmental condition. It involves differences in social communication, behavior and sensory processing. People on the spectrum are very different from one another.
Autistic person and person with autism
Both are used. Many autistic people prefer “autistic person” (identity-first), and others prefer “person with autism.” If you are unsure, ask what the person prefers.
Neurodiversity
The idea that differences in how brains work, including autism, are natural variation and not only problems to fix.
Neurodivergent and neurotypical
Neurodivergent describes people whose brains work in ways that differ from what is typical, such as autistic people. Neurotypical describes people whose brains work in the typical way.
Co-occurring conditions
Other health conditions that some autistic people also have, such as anxiety, depression, stomach and digestive problems, and sleep disorders. Doctors sometimes call these comorbid conditions.
Screening
A short check for signs that may mean a fuller assessment is worth doing. It does not give a diagnosis.
Diagnostic evaluation
A full assessment by qualified professionals to decide whether someone is autistic. Who does it and how long it takes varies by country.
Early intervention
Support services for very young children with developmental differences or delays. Rules and ages differ by country, so ask a doctor or local health service.
Sensory processing
How the body takes in and responds to sounds, light, touch, taste, smell and movement. Many autistic people are more or less sensitive than average to some of these.
Sensory overload
Feeling overwhelmed when there is too much sensory input at once, such as noise, bright lights or crowds.
Stimming
Repeated movements, sounds or actions, such as rocking or hand flapping, that people use to calm themselves, focus or express feelings.
Meltdown and shutdown
A meltdown is an intense reaction to being overwhelmed. It is not a tantrum. A shutdown is when someone withdraws, goes quiet or cannot respond. Both usually need calm, space and time.
Masking
Hiding or holding back natural autistic behavior to fit in. It can be exhausting over time.
Autistic burnout
Deep tiredness and reduced ability to cope after a long period of stress, often involving masking or too many demands.
Routine and transitions
Many autistic people find predictable routines comforting. Changes, or moving from one activity to another, can be hard and are easier with warning and a plan.
AAC (augmentative and alternative communication)
Tools and methods that help people communicate in ways other than speech, such as picture boards, apps or devices.
Occupational therapy
Therapy that helps people with everyday skills and activities, which can include sensory needs.
Speech and language therapy
Therapy that supports communication, including understanding, speaking and social communication.
Respite care
Short-term care that gives family caregivers a break.
Self-advocacy
Speaking up for your own needs, rights and choices. Autistic-led organizations often share resources on this.
IEP and similar school plans

In the United States, an Individualized Education Program is a written plan of school supports for eligible students. Other places use other names, such as an EHCP in England. Ask the school what applies.
Accommodations or adjustments
Changes to a school, workplace or place that make it easier to take part, such as a quiet space, written instructions or flexible hours.

topic_intro.signs: Autism looks different in every person. Common signs involve differences in social communication, behavior and sensory processing. These pages explain signs and point to information on screening and diagnosis.
topic_intro.diagnosis: A screening checks for signs that may mean a fuller assessment is worth doing. A diagnostic evaluation by qualified professionals decides whether someone is autistic. How to get one depends on where you live, and a good first step is to talk to a doctor you trust.
topic_intro.care: Support can include therapies such as speech and language therapy and occupational therapy. Decisions about care are best made with a qualified health professional who knows the person.
topic_intro.caregivers: Caring for an autistic person can be rewarding and tiring. Support for caregivers includes information, peer groups and short-term respite care.
topic_intro.mental: Anxiety, depression, sleep problems and stomach problems occur alongside autism for some people. A doctor can help look at what is going on and what support might help.
topic_intro.tech: Tools such as communication apps, visual schedules and wearable devices help some people. Look for tools that fit the person, and check the evidence and the privacy of any app.
topic_intro.advocacy: Self-advocacy means speaking up for your own needs, rights and choices. Autistic-led organizations share resources on rights, acceptance and reducing stigma.
topic_intro.daily: Routines, school, work and sensory needs shape everyday life. Planning ahead and asking for adjustments can make days easier.
topic_intro.local: Services such as clinics, therapy providers and support groups depend on where you live. Directories and local organizations can help you find them.
